subtopic: BROADCASTING-SALE OF RADIO STATION CKSB, WINNIPEG, TO CBC-ACTION TO SET ASIDE CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION COMMISSION DECISION
BROADCASTING-SALE OF RADIO STATION CKSB, WINNIPEG, TO CBC-ACTION TO SET ASIDE CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION COMMISSION DECISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments, in the brief time available to me, about a situation which has already been raised in the House on numerous occasions, namely, the takeover of radio station CKSB, Winnipeg, by the CBC. First I should like to make some comments about the Canadian RadioTelevision Commission itself. It appears to be most insensitive to the meaning and import of section 38 of the Official Languages Act and insensitive to the concept of multiculturalism as proclaimed by this government on several occasions in the past year and a half.
When the application was made to the CRTC and it was asked to consider the matter in Winnipeg, it decided to hold its meetings in Montreal. That decision was hard to understand; it did not make any sense at all. Representations were made to the CRTC prior to the meetings. Nevertheless, the commission insisted on holding the hearings, not in the city involved where people who were concerned could be present in sufficient numbers to make reasonable representations on their own behalf, but in another city, Montreal. I know that a few representatives travelled from Winnipeg-so far as I know, at government expense-to make representations but this was by no means satisfactory and did not obviate the need to hold hearings in Winnipeg where proper representations could have been made by all groups concerned.
I think the decision of the CRTC to allow this sale to go through constitutes blatant disregard of the established rights of the people in the Winnipeg area who have been accustomed to using this radio station for the purpose of third language broadcasts. I think the minister should explain to the House why the CRTC was so unreasonable in refusing to hold hearings in Winnipeg and, secondly, why he refused to direct the CRTC to the extent that he has any influence over it. The Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) is here this evening. I hope he will take this opportunity to explain what has happened.
We also had a communication from the Commissioner of Official Languages who was requested to investigate this takeover and see whether it was contrary to section 38 of the Official Languages Act. The commissioner's report indicated that station CKSB had been broadcasting in a third language for 20 years. In his report he repeatedly used the words "foreign languages". These words are offensive to Canadians who speak a language other than the two official languages; they object to having a third language referred to as a foreign language on so many occasions in the report of the Commissioner of Official Languages.
In any event, the commissioner concluded that in his opinion this takeover and the consequent loss of rights for ethnic groups with regard to the use of a third language in

May 31, 1973
Adjournment Debate
programming did not constitute an infraction of section 38 of the Official Languages Act. I am sorry to say that I have to disagree with the languages commissioner. He did not explain fully on what ground he made his deduction, and I hope he takes the opportunity to explain it in the near future.
In any event, the languages commissioner recommended that the CBC should reconsider its language policy and allow third language broadcasting. He made his point of view known to the CBC. The CBC replied in a negative manner; that is to say, they condescended to allow the use of this station to continue as at present for another year. In other words, it is to continue on a temporary basis. However, the CBC made it very plain to the languages commissioner that this concession that was granted to the ethnic groups concerned should not be considered by any means as a change in policy but only as a temporary arrangement, and it could not accede to the request of the languages commissioner to change its policy with respect to third language broadcasting.
The CBC has been hiding behind the Broadcasting Act on which it has based its policy. Section 3 of the act provides that all Canadians are entitled to broadcasting service in English and French as public funds become available. The CBC has considered broadcasting in English and French to be a priority. This does not mean that the CBC is not allowed to broadcast in other languages.
In this House there have been previous discussions on this subject with the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) and with the minister responsible for multiculturalism. We have also had discussions with the president of the CBC. We have obtained conflicting reports in that the president of the CBC has indicated that the Broadcasting Act does not really stand in the way in this matter; on the other hand, the Secretary of State has suggested that the Broadcasting Act does stand in the way of third language broadcasting. It is therefore my impression that arguments about legal principles and technicalities prevent third language broadcasting by the CBC. It is also my impression that nobody who so argues is at all interested in seeing that the ethnic groups involved receive justice. I think that is a shameful reflection on this government which claims to be concerned about all Canadians and says it is committed to a policy of multiculturalism. I think this matter ought to be straightened out forthwith.
A petition was presented to the governor in council a few days ago by the groups involved, asking that the government use its power to reverse the position taken by the CRTC in permitting this sale. They want the hearings to be held again in order that concerned groups can be heard. However, the government has refused to heed this petition and I should like to know why. I think the big fear created by this action is that it will set a precedent. If this action is allowed to go unchallenged, it is possible that other radio stations which now broadcast programs in a third language may follow the same course.
What will happen to stations in Regina, Saskatoon, Edmonton, Toronto and other parts of the country which are now broadcasting in a third language? Are these to go the same way? Will the languages commissioner claim

that established and customary rights have not been lost in all cases and refuse to take action? It is time the minister and the government were honest and gave us information as to where they really stand on this matter, to clarify once and for all the long-term prospects in third language broadcasting and the prospects for protecting established and customary rights as stated in Section 38 of the Official Languages Act.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member wants to give me the opportunity to explain the situation. I welcome this opportunity but I will use it mainly to inform the hon. member, who seems to ignore a great number of things pertaining to the question he has put forward tonight. The hon. member stated that the CRTC is insensitive and unreasonable about third languages. He has forgotten the policy the CRTC established for private stations over which it has authority, and in the field where it can make a policy outside the Broadcasting Act which concerns the CBC.
The hon. member blamed the CRTC for not holding the meeting in Winnipeg. This is very unfair, because the CRTC is the most mobile of all regulatory bodies in Canada. If the hon. member were reasonable, he would recognize that the CRTC cannot be in every city or town in this country at the same time. The hon. member must realize that there are problems pertaining to broadcasting and cablecasting in almost every city and town in this country at almost all times. It is absolutely impossible for them to be everywhere at the same time. It is very unfair to level such a charge against the CRTC which, I repeat, has been more mobile than any other regulatory body.
With regard to the petition that was presented to the governor in council, the hon. member can see no reason why the governor in council decided not to refer back to, or vary the decision of the CRTC. I must inform the hon. member that the petition was received so late that the cabinet would have had exactly 36 hours advance notice to review a question on which the CRTC had been holding hearings for days. It was entirely unreasonable to hope that within 36 hours the government would decide to reform, rescind or refer back the decision of the CRTC which had been very well motivated.
The CBC's language policy is another question. The CBC must interpret the law. It has legal advisers. It broadcasts in English and French. It cannot do any other broadcasting except at arm's length, in some northern parts, in native languages. The hon. member says we are committed to multiculturalism, but forgets the second part within a bilingual framework. When I was secretary of state and this policy was being developed, I met with many groups including the very interesting ethnic group to which the hon. member belongs. I asked whether they recognized the true terms of the policy of multiculturalism within a bilingual framework. Not one group in this country said no at that time. If they want to change their minds now, that is their absolute right. They can ask for a hearing before the CRTC at a place of their choice. They can hear the CBC, and their propositions can be considered-

subtopic: CANADA PENSION PLAN-HUTTERIAN BRETHREN OF CANADA-REQUEST FOR EXEMPTION FROM PAYING PREMIUMS
CANADA PENSION PLAN-HUTTERIAN BRETHREN OF CANADA-REQUEST FOR EXEMPTION FROM PAYING PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank the minister for his presence here tonight. The question I should like to deal with concerns Canada Pension Plan premiums paid by the Hutterian Brethren of Canada. Not only is the Department of National Health and Welfare concerned in the matter, but perhaps at this stage the Department of National Revenue is even more concerned; and I am sure the minister will convey my comments to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury).
The Hutterian Brethren are a minority group, a very unique group living in western Canada who in many instances, I feel, have been misunderstood, specifically with regard to the Canada Pension Plan. The Hutterian Brethren hold all things common. I should like to make it very clear to the minister that no individual can own any property, nor can he build up any personal equity, and a pension plan could be regarded as building up personal equity.
The Canada Pension Plan Act, section 6(2) (e), provides that "employment of a member of a religious order who has taken a vow of perpetual poverty and whose remuneration is paid either directly or by him to the order" is exempted from payment of Canada Pension Plan premiums. In their baptismal vows Hutterian Brethren are required to state;
That no one shall have any private possessions any more: for one gives and surrenders himself to the Lord and his church with all that he has and is able to do, as it was in the original apostolic church, when no one said of his possessions that they were his own, but all things were common to them.
According to a letter signed by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), the Hutterian Brethren of Canada were exempted from payment of CPP premiums as of January 1, 1972. In this regard I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) whether an amendment would be tabled or brought into the House to cover this provision by legislative action. In addition, there is a backlog of unpaid premiums from 1966 to the end of 1971. For six years, from the inception of the plan to the date the exemption took effect, these premiums have been accumulating on behalf of various Hutterian colonies in Manitoba.
I suggest that the collection of these fees is the whole nub of the matter. In the same letter to which I referred, the minister undertook not to take any action against the Hutterites to collect premiums without prior consultation with Hutterian representatives. Prior to 1972, when the exemption took effect, the Department of National Revenue took the tax refund credits which were to be paid to the Hutterian Brethren and placed them against the back premiums for those six years, at a time when the Hutterian Brethren had clearly been given to understand that no future collection action would be taken against them by the government without prior consultation. There was no prior consultation, yet this action was taken during a year
Adjournment Debate
when the Hutterian Brethren had been exempted by the government from paying premiums.
In conclusion, I ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of National Revenue to undertake a re-examination of this problem with the result that this inequity, in my view, can be removed in respect of the Hutterian Brethren.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to join the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) in paying tribute to the Hutterian Brethren of Canada for the contribution they have made to this country. They stand very high in the religious groups of this country in terms of their contribution to Canadian life. They bring to us a unique way of life, and have been in all respects exemplary citizens.

The problem raised by the hon. member has also been raised by the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Hymmen) for quite a while, and by the hon. member for Wellington-Grey-Dufferin-Waterloo (Mr. Beatty) on various occasions. When I was assigned to my present portfolio, and my colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) was assigned his portfolio last November, this was one issue drawn to our attention at that time. It has been decided that indeed we should do everything necessary to honour the commitment made by the former minister of national revenue. I have since been to the cabinet with my colleague, and I can tell the hon. member that this morning a bill was approved which I hope will be introduced in this House very shortly. I think it will remedy the situation raised by the hon. member to his satisfaction, and I hope we can receive unanimous support from all parties in the House in order that we might pass the bill in a very short time.
The bill includes four or five technical amendments to the Canada Pension Plan. The matter raised by the hon. member will be taken care of by these amendments. I hope the bill will be introduced within the next few days.

subtopic: ENERGY-PROPOSED WEST COAST OIL TANKER ROUTE-ALLEGED LACK OF DEPARTMENTAL CO-ORDINATION OF OPPOSITION
ENERGY-PROPOSED WEST COAST OIL TANKER ROUTE-ALLEGED LACK OF DEPARTMENTAL CO-ORDINATION OF OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue I raised in the form of a question to the hon. Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) appears at page 3131 of Hansard as follows:
Having in mind the criticism in recent days by the head of the Science Council of Canada, Dr. McTaggart-Cowan, of what he calls the snail's pace progress being made by the Minister of Transport and the Minister of the Environment to protect the west coast of British Columbia from potential oil spillage along the tanker route to Cherry Point, which is within 18 miles of my riding, is the minister satisfied with the protection that exists, or will he pay heed to the warning issued by the head of the Science Council within the last four or five days?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I will ever be completely satisfied with the measures that we are taking, but our performance recent-

May 31, 1973
Adjournment Debate
ly on the west coast relative to the spill from the freighter Irish Stardust was much better than that with respect to the Arrow with which Dr. McTaggart-Cowan is familiar.
British Columbians disagree on a great many more matters than we agree on, but if there is one thing on which we have unity it is the fact that it is inconceivable to us that Canada will not protect us from the inevitable major oil spills and massive pollution along our coast and the islands that will follow the shipment by giant oil tankers of oil from Alaska down the coast to Cherry Point, a refinery in Washington state about 18 miles from my riding. It is estimated there will be one such oil spill every four years.
With this in mind, I have tried to raise this issue as have other members representing the various parties. We do not need recapitulation of the whole situation tonight and, of course, time does not permit this. There is greater pressure now that safeguards be applied quickly, particularly in light of the fact that the United States is concerned about the need for energy, than there was maybe a year or two ago. This pressure is from environmentalists who recently managed to stay a U.S. project to move oil from Alaska by shipment along our coast.
The danger involved here to Alaska, and particularly to British Columbia, the lower mainland and the Gulf islands, is tremendous. The danger is great particularly in respect of these vast vessels, some of which are 100,000-ton tankers that I am told take almost a mile to change direction. This is an indication of the perils involved in their passage through the intricate and sometimes foggy channels just off the lower mainland of British Columbia and the Gulf islands of British Columbia. Therefore, I felt it was right to raise the matter again tonight.
The United States refinery at Cherry Point, which as I say is about 18 miles south of my riding, is an ecological time-bomb ticking away, one which will continue to tick away as long as the threat exists of these oil tankers bringing oil from Alaska down that coast to the refinery. I raise the question concerning what is being done to protect us because of the statement made by Dr. McTaggart-Cowan, an oil expert in this country if ever we had one. He has had experience on the east coast. He was very critical concerning the amount of action and effort, as well as success, of our departments of industry, trade and commerce, and transport to at least supply sort of a firefighter service to meet the situation if an oil spill should come about off the coast of British Columbia.
Last year Dr. McTaggart-Cowan said-I think he meant this in line with the suggestion that we cannot stop the oil shipments coming down the coast-"We will have to police the hell out of the oil tanker transports". A great many million dollars are at the disposal of both the Department of Transport and the Department of the Environment to cope with the many problems with which these departments are faced. I think a very small amount of this money is actually being used to police our west coast against the threat of oil pollution which would certainly result from oil tanker shipments down that coast.
I had the pleasure of questioning Dr. McTaggart-Cowan, head of the Science Council of Canada, on May 24 at a committee meeting. I asked him about his opinion of 
defensive measures being taken by the federal departments concerned. He replied to me in this way:
If you ask am I satisfied with the progress that has been made since Chedabucto Bay, the answer is no.
He went on to say:
This is not to say that people are not doing their best under a difficult situation, but international marine law is hopelessly inadequate. Canada cannot solve these problems alone .. . Having had the job of trying to cope with a few million gallons, no I will not be satisfied until the problem is licked and the problem is not licked by any manner of means. So the honest answer is no. I am restless. I wish I could see more action.
Coming from the source it did, I think this statement made a few weeks ago on this very grave problem in British Columbia deserves to be quoted tonight to underline the reason for my raising the question again with the minister, whom I know in many respects is a good minister who means very well. But I doubt that the people of British Columbia are satisfied with the action and practical application of money, men and machines to defend our shores-this is what it amounts to-from the threat of oil spill pollution which confronts us on the B.C. coast in particular.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: ENERGY-PROPOSED WEST COAST OIL TANKER ROUTE-ALLEGED LACK OF DEPARTMENTAL CO-ORDINATION OF OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing that British Columbians can agree on, it is the necessity to protect our coasts from oil spills, particulary spills resulting from the movement of Alaskan oil down the west coast by supertanker. We must prevent the spills from occurring in the first place. We will, however, have some spills in our own waters simply because there oil and other products are moving in relatively small quantities up and down the coast to remote locations.
Therefore we must be ready to deal with emergency situation first in respect of the prevention of massive oil spills. For example, through the United Nations at Stockholm last June we managed to have resolutions passed- and, incidentally, the United States and a great majority of nations were with us-which were opposed to the shipment of oil in large quantities through inland areas, parts of the world in which ocean or waters were contained, parts of the world in which navigation would be difficult and parts of the world where the biological flora and fauna were unique or precious or where recreation and tourism were important. Certainly the waters between the mainland of B.C. and Vancouver Island fall within that category.
We have entered, with the United States, into a joint contingency plan to deal with spills should they occur, but our basic approach is to prevent large tankers from coming into those waters at all. Basically, the answer is to continue to supply refineries in the Seattle and Vancouver areas by pipeline from western Canada, and if Alaskan oil does move down the west coast of North America it should go to California, which is its principal destination in any case. In other words, we should keep the big trucks on the highways of the seas and not bring them in too close to parkland areas close to Vancouver. That must be the basic policy.
But we also have environmental emergency centres established across the country. In other words, there is a

phone number which can be called by anyone but especially by federal government departments and provincial administrations as well as by U.S. coastguards and others. We have worked out a co-operative agreement with the United States coastguard and we have been assembling a lot of equipment. We have a $5 million program to have sticklicks on hand and oil booms; we have the little Pisces submarine out there, and so on.
Adjournment Debate
Dr. McTaggart-Cowan is a competent gentleman who has had a lot of experience with the Arrow oil spill. We welcome him back to take a look at our new organization, our new arrangements and our equipment on the west coast at any time. I think he will agree that we have made progress. But I must repeat what I said to the hon. member earlier. Personally, I am not satisfied we have reached the millennium-we have still quite a long way to go.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
